power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Using Vision and Large Language Models for Psychological Intervention Competency Assessment: A Pilot Study of Agreement with Clinician Ratings

text.text: Introduction: Supervision in psychological intervention training is limited by the time needed to evaluate simulated sessions.
We tested a Vision Language Model (VLM) and Large Language Model (LLM) pipeline that assesses competency from verbal and nonverbal communication.
Method: Gemini-3.1-Pro was used to annotate behaviors in 25 simulated therapy videos and incorporate them into transcripts, and ChatGPT-6.1-Sol rated them against the ENACT scale.
Two clinicians verified VLM-identified behaviors and four independently rated each video.
Agreement was estimated with Gwet's AC1 and ICC.
Results: Of 1,558 VLM-identified behaviors, 70% were confirmed by both clinicians and 93% by at least one.
AI-clinician agreement on therapeutic behavior attributes (AC1=0.73, 95% CI 0.70-0.76) approached between-clinician agreement (0.75, 0.72-0.78).
AI-clinician ICCs on therapeutic domain levels (median 0.57) were modestly lower than between-clinician ICCs (0.67).
Discussion: The pipeline agreed with clinicians nearly as well as clinicians agreed with each other and shows promise as a supplementary evaluator in therapist training.

The prevalence of depression among adolescents and adults in the United States rose from 8.2% in 2013-2014 to 13.1% in 2021-2023, [1] and diagnosed anxiety among children increased by 29% between 2016 and 2020, [2] raising demand for evidence-based psychological interventions that the clinical workforce has not met.
text.formatted: The prevalence of depression among adolescents and adults in the United States rose from 8.2% in 2013-2014 to 13.1% in 2021-2023, <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> and diagnosed anxiety among children increased by 29% between 2016 and 2020, <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> raising demand for evidence-based psychological interventions that the clinical workforce has not met.

text.text: About 137 million Americans live in federally designated mental health professional shortage areas, with a projected shortfall of 21,480 mental health counselors in 2026. [3] Scaling up psychological interventions is one response to this gap, but expanding this workforce depends on supervised training, in which a supervisor watches each simulated session, rates it against a structured rubric, and documents feedback, so the supply of supervisors and the time per review constrain how many trainees can be trained and how often they receive feedback.
text.formatted: About 137 million Americans live in federally designated mental health professional shortage areas, with a projected shortfall of 21,480 mental health counselors in 2026. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> Scaling up psychological interventions is one response to this gap, but expanding this workforce depends on supervised training, in which a supervisor watches each simulated session, rates it against a structured rubric, and documents feedback, so the supply of supervisors and the time per review constrain how many trainees can be trained and how often they receive feedback.

text.text: Global efforts in task sharing of psychological interventions offer a model for scaling provider training and competency assessment.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed brief, scalable psychological interventions, which use elements of cognitive behavioral therapy for communities with limited specialist providers. [4] The accompanying implementation manual guides the integration of these interventions into existing services and treats workforce preparation as a core step in expanding access to care.
text.formatted: The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed brief, scalable psychological interventions, which use elements of cognitive behavioral therapy for communities with limited specialist providers. <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> The accompanying implementation manual guides the integration of these interventions into existing services and treats workforce preparation as a core step in expanding access to care.

text.text: As the non-specialist workforce expands, competency-based training becomes essential to the quality of care.

New providers must demonstrate foundational helping skills, such as rapport building and nonverbal communication, as well as intervention-specific skills, such as problem solving or behavioral activation.

The training needs of non-specialist providers are easily underestimated, [5] and the supervision they require falls on specialists who already carry high caseloads, so reducing the supervision burden is a condition for scaling this model of care.
text.formatted: The training needs of non-specialist providers are easily underestimated, <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> and the supervision they require falls on specialists who already carry high caseloads, so reducing the supervision burden is a condition for scaling this model of care.

text.text: Automating the evaluation with artificial intelligence (AI) could relieve this training and supervision bottleneck.
Existing AI approaches to rating therapist competence or fidelity have worked from transcripts alone, [6] [7] [8] which carry only conversational content.
text.formatted: Existing AI approaches to rating therapist competence or fidelity have worked from transcripts alone, <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> which carry only conversational content.

text.text: Eye contact, facial expressions, gestures, posture, and tone of voice are central to rapport building [9] and carry important assessment cues for various competency domains, so a rating built from dialogue alone cannot provide the evidence those domains require.
text.formatted: Eye contact, facial expressions, gestures, posture, and tone of voice are central to rapport building <ref type="bibr">[9]</ref> and carry important assessment cues for various competency domains, so a rating built from dialogue alone cannot provide the evidence those domains require.

text.text: Recent developments in Vision Language Models (VLMs) and Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a way to address this challenge.
VLMs accept images and audio and can describe visual and vocal behaviors alongside the spoken content, converting a video into a text record of verbal and nonverbal communication.
LLMs can evaluate text consistently against a pre-specified rubric, applying the same criteria to every session.

Separating perception from judgment also makes the assessment auditable, since the behavior-annotated transcript is a record that a supervisor can check against the video and to which each rating can be traced.

We therefore tested a VLM+LLM pipeline on simulated therapy sessions, asking whether the VLM captures verbal and nonverbal communication accurately and whether LLM ratings of the resulting transcripts agree with clinician ratings.

We compiled 25 publicly available videos of simulated therapy sessions from YouTube, 2 to 32 minutes long, comprising 11 intake sessions, 4 motivational interviewing sessions, and 10 demonstrations of flawed counseling skills (selection criteria in Table S1, video details in Table S2).
text.formatted: We compiled 25 publicly available videos of simulated therapy sessions from YouTube, 2 to 32 minutes long, comprising 11 intake sessions, 4 motivational interviewing sessions, and 10 demonstrations of flawed counseling skills (selection criteria in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>, video details in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S2</ref>).

text.text: The flawed-skill videos were purposively selected so that unhelpful or potentially harmful behaviors would be represented.

We used the ENhancing Assessment of Common Therapeutic factors (ENACT) (English, in-person, v1.0), which was developed for training and supervision of psychological treatments and has shown acceptable validity and inter-rater reliability. [10] For each therapeutic domain, ENACT lists binary behavior attributes grouped as unhelpful or potentially harmful behaviors, basic helping skills, and advanced helping skills.
text.formatted: We used the ENhancing Assessment of Common Therapeutic factors (ENACT) (English, in-person, v1.0), which was developed for training and supervision of psychological treatments and has shown acceptable validity and inter-rater reliability. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> For each therapeutic domain, ENACT lists binary behavior attributes grouped as unhelpful or potentially harmful behaviors, basic helping skills, and advanced helping skills.

text.text: Each domain also receives a level from 1 to 4, with higher levels indicating stronger competency.

Clinicians assigned domain levels by holistic judgment, whereas the LLM derived each level from the attributes it marked present by applying explicit scoring rules adapted based on clinician practices (Table S3).
text.formatted: Clinicians assigned domain levels by holistic judgment, whereas the LLM derived each level from the attributes it marked present by applying explicit scoring rules adapted based on clinician practices (Table <ref type="table">S3</ref>).

text.text: We excluded Domain 7 (Assessment of Harm and Developing Response Plan) because harm management requires dedicated sessions and could not be assessed in our material.
Six Qualified Behavioral Health Specialists employed at Nationwide Children's Hospital volunteered as evaluators.
Evaluators had between 16 and 22 months of clinical experience and used the ENACT weekly in clinical supervision.
Two evaluators verified VLM-identified behaviors, and the other four rated the videos against the ENACT.
We used the VLM Gemini-3.1-Pro via API to capture verbal and nonverbal communication in simulated therapy videos.
Each video or selected clip was input at one frame per second with its audio track, title, and metadata.

The VLM was prompted to transcribe the dialogue and to annotate timestamped behaviors, labeling each as descriptive (directly observable) or interpretative (inferring emotion or interactional function).
We used the LLM ChatGPT-6.1-Sol via API to rate the behavior-annotated transcripts against the ENACT.

For each domain, the LLM marked each behavior attribute as present or absent, assigned a domain level based on specified rules, and provided scoring rationale by citing timestamped evidence from the transcript.
Attributes and levels could be rated Not Assessable (NA) when the transcript offered no opportunity to demonstrate the skill.
Model access details and full prompts are in Table S3.
text.formatted: Model access details and full prompts are in Table <ref type="table">S3</ref>.

text.text: In the pipeline (Figure 1), the VLM processed each video into a behavior-annotated transcript, the LLM rated each transcript against the ENACT, and two human evaluation tasks proceeded in parallel.
text.formatted: In the pipeline (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>), the VLM processed each video into a behavior-annotated transcript, the LLM rated each transcript against the ENACT, and two human evaluation tasks proceeded in parallel.

text.text: Two evaluators judged whether each VLM-identified behavior was present in the original video, and four evaluators independently rated every video against the ENACT, blinded to the transcripts and AI ratings.
All raters evaluated the videos in the same order and could view video titles and metadata.
All analyses were conducted in R 4.6.0 with the irr and irrCAC packages. [11] [12] [13] VLM behavior precision.
text.formatted: All analyses were conducted in R 4.6.0 with the irr and irrCAC packages. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> VLM behavior precision.

text.text: Precision was defined as the percentage of VLM-identified behaviors confirmed by the two human evaluators.
We report it under a strict criterion (both evaluators confirmed) and a lenient criterion (at least one evaluator confirmed).

Agreement between the two evaluators was summarized with Gwet's AC1, [14] with thresholds defined as slight (<0.2), fair (0.2-0.4), moderate (0.4-0.6), substantial (0.6-0.8), and excellent (0.8-1.0). [15] Behavior rating agreement.
text.formatted: Agreement between the two evaluators was summarized with Gwet's AC1, <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> with thresholds defined as slight (<0.2), fair (0.2-0.4), moderate (0.4-0.6), substantial (0.6-0.8), and excellent (0.8-1.0). <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> Behavior rating agreement.

text.text: Between-clinician and AI-clinician agreement on ENACT binary behavior attributes was calculated with Gwet's AC1, overall and separately for harmful behaviors (only in videos selected to demonstrate them), basic skills, and advanced skills.

AC1 was computed on video-attribute ratings pooled across videos, using the multi-rater form across four clinicians for between-clinician agreement and the four AI-clinician pairs stacked together for AI-clinician agreement.
Because the clinician checklist does not include a not-assessable option, behaviors the AI rated as NA were treated as absent.

Agreement on the 1-4 ENACT domain level was estimated with a one-way, single-measure intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC(1)), interpreted with the same thresholds as AC1. [15] Blank clinician levels and AI NA ratings were treated as not assessable.
text.formatted: Agreement on the 1-4 ENACT domain level was estimated with a one-way, single-measure intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC(1)), interpreted with the same thresholds as AC1. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> Blank clinician levels and AI NA ratings were treated as not assessable.

text.text: ICC was computed on all rater pairs stacked together, keeping only pairs in which both raters gave a valid level.
Primary analyses only included domains with valid clinician and AI ratings in more than 20 videos.
Confidence intervals.
95% CIs for AC1 and ICC were bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) bootstrap intervals (2,000 resamples of videos), which adjust for skewness in bounded agreement coefficients. [16]
text.formatted: 95% CIs for AC1 and ICC were bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) bootstrap intervals (2,000 resamples of videos), which adjust for skewness in bounded agreement coefficients. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>

text.text: The VLM identified 1,558 behaviors across the 25 videos, most of them descriptive, with gestures, head movements, and visual attention accounting for most annotations and vocal cues and interpersonal distance rarely captured (Table 1).
text.formatted: The VLM identified 1,558 behaviors across the 25 videos, most of them descriptive, with gestures, head movements, and visual attention accounting for most annotations and vocal cues and interpersonal distance rarely captured (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The number of behaviors per video ranged from 20 to 146, and behavior density was higher in short clips demonstrating unhelpful behaviors than in full-length intake sessions (Table S4).
text.formatted: The number of behaviors per video ranged from 20 to 146, and behavior density was higher in short clips demonstrating unhelpful behaviors than in full-length intake sessions (Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: Overall, 70% of VLM-identified behaviors were confirmed by both evaluators (strict criterion) and 93% by at least one (lenient criterion).
Interpretative behaviors had higher precision than descriptive behaviors under both criteria (strict 78.2% vs.
68.5%, lenient 99.4% vs.
Among descriptive categories, strict precision was highest for eye contact (88.8%) and lowest for body posture (37.0%), and lenient precision was at least 85.0% in every category (Table 2).
text.formatted: Among descriptive categories, strict precision was highest for eye contact (88.8%) and lowest for body posture (37.0%), and lenient precision was at least 85.0% in every category (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: The two evaluators showed substantial agreement in confirming VLM-identified behaviors (overall AC1 0.67, 95% CI 0.63-0.71).
Agreement was similar for interpretative behaviors (0.74, 0.64-0.83) and descriptive behaviors (0.66, 0.62-0.70), with overlapping confidence intervals.
The difference between strict and lenient precision therefore reflects disagreement between evaluators about what the video shows as much as it reflects VLM error.
The LLM completed each evaluation in a median of 64s (range: 53-84s) at a cost of $0.07-$0.09 per video (Table S4).
text.formatted: The LLM completed each evaluation in a median of 64s (range: 53-84s) at a cost of $0.07-$0.09 per video (Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: Across all binary ENACT behavior attributes, AI-clinician agreement was substantial (AC1 0.73, 95% CI 0.70-0.76) and close to between-clinician agreement (0.75, 0.72-0.78) (Figure 2).
text.formatted: Across all binary ENACT behavior attributes, AI-clinician agreement was substantial (AC1 0.73, 95% CI 0.70-0.76) and close to between-clinician agreement (0.75, 0.72-0.78) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: The two comparisons were also comparable within behavior subcategories.
For unhelpful or potentially harmful behaviors, AI-clinician agreement (0.65, 0.54-0.76) was slightly higher than between-clinician agreement (0.59, 0.49-0.71).

Agreement was substantial for advanced helping skills (between-clinician 0.73, 0.60-0.84, AI-clinician 0.73, 0.61-0.82) and moderate for basic helping skills (between-clinician 0.59, 0.54-0.68, AI-clinician 0.53, 0.47-0.61).
In every category, AI-clinician agreement was within 0.07 of between-clinician agreement, and the bootstrapped confidence intervals of the two comparisons overlapped.
The AI rated two domains not assessable more often than clinicians did, providing valid levels in 13 videos for Confidentiality and 14 for Rapport Building.

These classifications were concentrated in the motivational interviewing and flawed-skill videos, which begin mid-session, and they follow from the LLM prompt, which instructed the model to treat introductions and a confidentiality briefing as not assessable when a session was not a first meeting.
The AI's NA ratings therefore follow a consistent, prompt-defined rule.
Clinicians received no equivalent instruction, and their blank levels varied considerably across individuals, with one clinician accounting for most of them.
These blank levels more likely reflect individual practice than a shared criterion (Table S5).
text.formatted: These blank levels more likely reflect individual practice than a shared criterion (Table <ref type="table">S5</ref>).

text.text: In other ENACT domains, between-clinician ICCs ranged from moderate to excellent (0.43-0.93) and were substantial in 8 of 12 domains (Figure 3).
text.formatted: In other ENACT domains, between-clinician ICCs ranged from moderate to excellent (0.43-0.93) and were substantial in 8 of 12 domains (Figure <ref type="figure">3</ref>).

text.text: AI-clinician ICCs ranged from moderate to substantial (0.46-0.70).
Overall, AI-clinician agreement was modestly lower than between-clinician agreement (median ICC 0.57 vs.
The largest discrepancy was observed for Verbal Communication, where between-clinician agreement was excellent (0.93), the highest of any domain, and AI-clinician agreement was only moderate (0.55).
In Family Involvement and Coping Mechanisms, AI agreed better with clinicians than clinicians agreed with each other (0.56 vs.
Table S6 presents ICCs with 95% CIs for all domains assessed.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">S6</ref> presents ICCs with 95% CIs for all domains assessed.

text.text: This pilot study evaluated a pipeline combining a Vision Language Model and a Large Language Model to assess psychological intervention competency in simulated therapy sessions.

Most VLM-identified behaviors were verified in the original videos, and the AI ENACT ratings agreed substantially with clinicians on binary behavior attributes and moderately to substantially on domain levels, comparable to or modestly below between-clinician agreement.
These results should be read against the variability of the human benchmark.

Clinicians did not align perfectly in behavior confirmation (AC1=0.67), attribute presence (AC1=0.75), or domain-level rating (ICC 0.43-0.93), indicating they interpret video content and ENACT criteria differently.

Because no single clinician provides a definitive reference standard, consistency among clinicians sets a practical upper bound on the agreement any rater, human or automated, can reach. [15] The VLM+LLM pipeline came close to this agreement upper bound on behavior attributes and fell modestly short on domain levels.
text.formatted: Because no single clinician provides a definitive reference standard, consistency among clinicians sets a practical upper bound on the agreement any rater, human or automated, can reach. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> The VLM+LLM pipeline came close to this agreement upper bound on behavior attributes and fell modestly short on domain levels.

text.text: It can therefore be positioned as an additional rater whose judgments fall within the range of disagreement already present among clinicians, rather than as a substitute for them.

The pipeline applies the same criteria to every session without fatigue, requires little manual effort beyond recording and uploading sessions, and produces standardized ratings with timestamped behaviorannotated transcripts that are easier to store, search, and audit than raw video.
Processing and rating each video took under 6 minutes and cost less than $1, for a total of about $12 across 247 minutes of footage (Table S4).
text.formatted: Processing and rating each video took under 6 minutes and cost less than $1, for a total of about $12 across 247 minutes of footage (Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: Because each rating is supported by time-stamped evidence from the transcript, supervisors can verify ratings quickly and focus their review where human judgment is most needed.
These findings have practical implications for how the pipeline can be integrated into clinical training and supervision.

Competence in psychological interventions develops through repeated practice with specific and timely feedback, [17] and the supervisors who can provide such feedback are a limited resource in most training settings. [18] An automated evaluator that returns rubric-anchored and evidence-linked feedback after every session can potentially change the frequency of feedback that trainees receive (e.g., feedback on each simulated session rather than on a sample of sessions), which may support skill acquisition over the course of training.
text.formatted: Competence in psychological interventions develops through repeated practice with specific and timely feedback, <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> and the supervisors who can provide such feedback are a limited resource in most training settings. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> An automated evaluator that returns rubric-anchored and evidence-linked feedback after every session can potentially change the frequency of feedback that trainees receive (e.g., feedback on each simulated session rather than on a sample of sessions), which may support skill acquisition over the course of training.

text.text: However, the use of automated ratings should remain formative at this stage.
Observer-rated competence has shown only modest associations with client outcomes, [19] which indicates that an automated rating is an indicator for training instead of a warrant of quality.
text.formatted: Observer-rated competence has shown only modest associations with client outcomes, <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> which indicates that an automated rating is an indicator for training instead of a warrant of quality.

text.text: Therefore, its use in certification or employment decisions should be deferred until its relationship with outcomes has been examined.

Transcript-based fidelity feedback has been found feasible and acceptable to therapists and community mental health supervisors, [20] and a similar implementation path can be expected for a multimodal evaluator.
text.formatted: Transcript-based fidelity feedback has been found feasible and acceptable to therapists and community mental health supervisors, <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> and a similar implementation path can be expected for a multimodal evaluator.

text.text: Here, feedback could be delivered to the trainee after each session, and supervisor review is reserved for flagged sessions.
Such an approach can potentially place clinician expertise where disagreement is most informative, instead of requiring supervisor review across every session.
The results also point to where the pipeline should change.

The VLM annotated behavior categories unevenly, body posture had the lowest precision, and vocal cues accounted for only 26 of 1,558 annotations even though the prompt named tone, pace, pauses, and silence as a category to capture, so the transcript carried almost no indication about how a message was verbally conveyed or person selfexpressed.

This sparsity is a plausible source of the largest divergence in domain levels, since clinicians agreed almost perfectly on Verbal Communication (ICC 0.93) while hearing the sessions, whereas the LLM rated it from text with little paralinguistic evidence (0.55).

Because prompting alone did not elicit paralinguistic annotation, a separate audio pass or acoustic features extracted independently of the visual stream may be needed, and a behavior list derived from the ENACT attributes rather than improvised for this pilot would align annotation with the cues the rubric scores.

In general, clinicians agreed more with each other than with the AI on domain levels, which may reflect a shared understanding of the criteria, built through clinical training, that the prompt does not capture.
Several constraints bound these inferences.

The sample was small, covered three session types, and consisted of public videos of simulated sessions that varied in length, resolution, and recording angle, so generalization to recorded clinical sessions is untested.

Although clinicians rated without access to transcripts or AI ratings, neither they nor the models were blinded to video titles and metadata, and because several titles announce flawed practice, both could infer the intended quality of a session, which may have inflated agreement on harmful behaviors in particular.
The evaluators were early-career clinicians who use ENACT routinely, so the benchmark reflects trained routine raters rather than experienced supervisors.

We assessed precision but not recall of VLM-identified behaviors, and each video was processed once at a sampling temperature of 1, so missed behaviors remain unquantified and the stability of AI ratings across runs and model versions is unknown.

The comparison is one of agreement rather than accuracy, since no reference standard for competency exists beyond clinician judgment, and VLM identification of cues such as eye contact and interpersonal distance may carry cultural assumptions that these sessions did not test.

Next steps are to refine the prompts, assess recall and repeat-run stability, test alternative models, and scale to standardized simulated sessions recorded in a hospital training program, where any extension to real sessions would require privacy-preserving, on-premise model deployment.

In conclusion, an automated VLM-LLM pipeline produced competency ratings that agreed with clinicians nearly as well as clinicians agreed with each other, and could serve as an additional evaluator in therapist training once its recall and its performance on recorded clinical sessions have been established.
This could help expand access to psychological interventions as the workforce scales up using task sharing approaches.
All available data has been presented with the publication.
